source.title: Polysemanticity and Capacity in Neural Networks
source.authors: Adam Scherlis; Kshitij Sachan; A. Jermyn; Joe Benton; Buck Shlegeris

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices and references, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests toy-model feature capacity, sparsity and embedding geometry, but uses a different main toy model and objective from the original superposition study.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own analytical and numerical toy-model results and a geometric characterization of efficient embedding matrices. Statements explicitly attributed to prior work, including earlier empirical findings about Anthropic's model geometry, are not recorded as this paper's results.
record.test_reason: The paper analyses and numerically trains its own quadratic-activation toy model, and reruns Anthropic's toy model. It reports when features are ignored, shared (superposed) or fully represented as sparsity and importance vary, and the geometry of efficient embeddings. These results bear directly on V1 and V2 in toy settings. The main model and objective (nonlinear computation, not compression) differ from the original, hence T2.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly correct. It should add three points: optimal allocation follows each feature's marginal loss reduction, which explains features pinned at capacity 0 or 1. The phase diagram agrees qualitatively with that of Toy Models of Superposition. And the quadratic model always gives one large block, whereas the original found a range of block sizes, suggesting architecture controls how much polysemanticity appears.
record.recipe_differences: The main model is a two-layer quadratic-activation regression model for a nonlinear computation, rather than the original autoencoder data-compression setup; the paper also numerically compares phase diagrams with the Anthropic toy model.
record.method_sensitivity: The phase diagram changes with input kurtosis/sparsity and feature importance; the paper also reports differences with activation function, toy-model architecture, and feature-to-dimension ratio.
record.problems: Evidence is limited to toy models and analytic assumptions; the numerical phase diagrams are reported qualitatively without uncertainty estimates. The paper does not test LLMs. Its comparison also shows architecture-dependent outcomes, limiting generalization from one toy model.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying results left out. Earlier empirical claims about Anthropic's embedding geometry are attributed to prior work and were excluded.

untested.parts: Only small toy models (6 features in 3 or 5 dimensions, plus the analytic N-in-D case). No empirical pairwise-angle measurements are reported.
Whether capacity competition explains polysemantic neurons in real trained networks or LLMs.
Not tested. The paper names rotated embeddings as another cause of polysemanticity but explicitly does not study it.
Not tested: no LLM or SAE results.
Not tested. The paper assumes each scalar feature is a single embedding direction and never compares this with multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: In Anthropic's model a large region has capacity stuck near 1/2, which the authors read as antipodal pairs; capacity in their own model changes smoothly. Their model also has a narrower superposed region than Anthropic's.
Analytic and empirical phase diagrams agree for the 6-features-in-3-neurons quadratic model.

record.verdict_notes: The evidence is mostly analytic, with qualitative numerical phase diagrams and no uncertainty estimates. The reader's V6 links and V6 'supports' label are dropped: treating features as 1-D directions is an assumption of the setup, not a test. A researcher should note that r3 and r4 come from the authors' rerun of the original model.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test LLMs or establish that the same geometry holds across real models; the paper notes that its quadratic model and Anthropic's autoencoder model have different phase diagrams and block structures.
Tests capacity allocation in toy models, not whether this mechanism explains polysemanticity in trained LLMs.
Does not test non-capacity causes of polysemanticity or whether polysemanticity alone is evidence of superposition.
No LLM feature-distribution or sparse-autoencoder results.
Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable or canonical representation units.
Studies scalar input features represented by embedding vectors in toy models; it does not compare that setup with multidimensional features or test feature dimensionality in LLMs.

rows.subject: quadratic model
rows.size_stated: 6 features and 3 neurons for Figure 4; general N features and D dimensions in the analysis
rows.operation_detail: Analytically derives and numerically illustrates optimal feature-capacity allocation as feature importance and kurtosis vary.

conditions.value: one feature's relative importance varies against the others

rows.measure: Optimal capacity allocated to each feature
rows.value: For k > 3, sufficiently unimportant features are ignored, sufficiently important features are fully represented, and an intermediate range receives fractional capacity; for k ≤ 3, features are either ignored or fully represented. The intermediate, partially represented region occurs at higher sparsity.
rows.note: The paper gives analytic thresholds in terms of k, feature importance vi, and the Lagrange multiplier λ; the row summarizes the stated regimes rather than transcribing the equations.

rows.subject: our toy model
rows.size_stated: 6 features in 3 dimensions displayed; 6 features in 5 dimensions also studied
rows.operation_detail: Compares numerical capacity-allocation phase diagrams across activation functions.

conditions.value: 6 in 3 displayed; the text says 6 in 5 is similar

rows.value: The paper reports a sharp 0–1 transition at mild sparsity and a smoother transition with a superposition region at higher sparsity; it says the same general shape appears across the studied nonlinearities.
rows.note: The reported trend is qualitative; plotted phase-diagram values are not given numerically in the text.

rows.subject: Anthropic toy model [EHO+ 22b]
rows.operation_detail: Compares the model's numerical capacity-allocation phase diagram with the authors' toy model.

conditions.value: one feature can be orders of magnitude more important than the others

rows.measure: Feature capacity in the phase diagram
rows.value: For the 6-in-3 case, the paper reports that features can remain in superposition even when their importance is orders of magnitude greater than any other feature.
rows.note: The paper describes this as a difference from its own model, where this outcome does not occur.
rows.check: This row reports Anthropic's 6-in-3 model keeping a feature superposed even when it is orders of magnitude more important. That runs against V2's claim that important features get dedicated dimensions, so V2 holds only partially here. It says nothing new about V1's sparsity transition, so the V1 link is removed. The run is the authors' own numerical rerun, so it is a legitimate row.

rows.subject: Anthropic toy model [EHO+ 22b]
rows.operation_detail: Compares the numerical capacity-allocation phase diagram in the one-extra-feature setting.

conditions.value: one feature's importance varies relative to the others

rows.measure: Whether a feature remains partially represented when much more important than the others
rows.value: The paper says the high-importance superposition outcome described for 6 in 3 does not occur when there is only one more feature than neurons.
rows.note: This is a stated contrast between feature-to-dimension settings; the text does not give a numerical threshold.
rows.check: The state was wrong. In the 6-in-5 setting the high-importance superposition does not occur, so the important feature gets its own dimension as V2 predicts: observed, not partial. The V1 link is removed.

rows.subject: efficient embedding matrices
rows.size_stated: D dimensions and N features, with total capacity saturated
rows.operation_detail: Characterizes the geometry of matrices that saturate the total-capacity bound.

conditions.value: efficient matrices with total capacity equal to D

rows.value: The paper proves that efficient matrices have a block-semiorthogonal form. Features interfere within a block but not across blocks; a feature reaching capacity 1 becomes orthogonal and separates into a new block.
rows.note: This is a mathematical characterization, not an empirical estimate of pairwise angles. It allows blocks of different sizes and does not imply all overlapping vectors are nearly orthogonal to one another.
rows.check: This is a theorem (all efficient matrices are block-semiorthogonal), not an empirical measurement. Small blocks correspond to regular polytopes, which bears on V1's geometry. It does not compare 1-D with multi-dimensional features, so the V6 link is removed.

rows.subject: our quadratic model
rows.operation_detail: Reports the block structure of embedding matrices in the quadratic toy model.
rows.measure: Number and structure of embedding-matrix blocks
rows.value: The paper states that its model's embedding matrices have one large superposed block, except for ignored or fully represented features.
rows.note: The paper contrasts this with prior reported findings for Anthropic's model; those cited findings are not recorded here as this study's own result.
rows.check: The quadratic model always has one large, 'less-ordered' superposed block, not regular polytope motifs. Superposition is present but V1's regular geometry is not, so the state is partial. The V6 link is removed.

statements.correction: k<3: no partial representation. k=3 at equal importance: any capacity allocation saturating the dimension bound is optimal, including superposition. k>3: an intermediate superposition region exists. Efficient embeddings are block-semiorthogonal.
statements.problem: The categorical k≤3 description follows Section 3.4 but omits Section 3.6's explicit critical-point exception.

statements.correction: k<3: features are ignored or fully represented. At k=3 with equal importance, shared allocations can also be optimal. The remaining allocation, architecture-comparison and geometry claims agree with the text.
